revisions.title: The logos begins after the punishment argument
revisions.body: Punishment is the proof Protagoras has just completed, not the logos he is about to begin. He argues that reasoned punishment looks to the future—to deter the offender and educate witnesses—so Athenians treat virtue as teachable. At 324d he marks a new turn: the remaining problem will be answered with a logos rather than a mythos.

revisions.title: Keep the speaker handoff in view
revisions.body: At 328a the voice shifts: Socrates introduces the craftsmen’s-sons comparison, asking who could teach sons the crafts learned from fathers and fellow practitioners. He uses that comparison to test how virtue can be taught. Protagoras resumes by presenting himself as someone who can advance a learner even a little. Keep the analogy with Socrates and the self-endorsement with Protagoras.

body: "Protagoras shifts the problem from finding a single source of virtue to recognizing a distributed civic formation. His analogy with craftsmen’s sons suggests that people already acquire a practice through family and fellow practitioners; virtue likewise belongs to a community in which everyone teaches as far as he can. The specialist is not thereby unnecessary, but his advantage is harder to isolate: he is the one who advances someone even a little."
